paper.title: Cardiometabolic Risk Factors in Women Exposed to High Altitude.

problem.title: Women's cardiometabolic responses to high-altitude exposure are poorly understood, leaving them vulnerable to altitude-related illness.
problem.summary: An increasing number of women live, work, and engage in athletic activity at high altitude, yet little is known about how sex-specific factors such as the menstrual cycle, contraceptive use, pregnancy, and menopause interact with cardiometabolic risk in these environments. This lack of knowledge may contribute to impaired acclimatization and increased risk of altitude-related illness in women. The review synthesizes existing evidence to identify knowledge gaps and guide future research.
problem.affected_women: Women exposed to high altitude through occupational, athletic, or residential settings.

data_need.description: Data on physiological and cardiometabolic adaptations of women at high altitude, including how menstrual cycle, contraceptive use, pregnancy, and menopause affect acclimatization.
data_need.why_it_matters: Without this data, prevention, acclimatization strategies, and clinical management for women at high altitude cannot be properly informed, potentially increasing their risk of altitude-related illness.

gap_evidence.note: The abstract states 'little is known about the physiological adaptations experienced by women at high altitude, particularly regarding metabolic alterations that may contribute to impaired acclimatization,' and that the review aims to 'identify existing knowledge gaps' in this area.

dataset_source.note: Covers menstrual-cycle-phase effects on cardiorespiratory/exercise responses at high altitude (Sci Rep 2024) and menstrual cycle/menopause/progesterone effects on acute mountain sickness (Wilderness Environ Med 2024), plus a broader narrative review of hormonal life-course effects on hypoxia responses. Does NOT constitute a large-scale primary dataset on cardiometabolic adaptation across menstrual cycle, contraceptive use, pregnancy, and menopause combined; pregnancy-specific and chronic long-term acclimatization data at altitude remain limited.

verification.findings: This exact knowledge gap comes from the review 'Cardiometabolic Risk Factors in Women Exposed to High Altitude' (PubMed 42511692 / PMC13410897), which itself synthesizes existing evidence rather than reflecting a total void. Since related work has begun to fill parts of the gap: a 2024 Scientific Reports study examined menstrual-cycle-phase effects on cardiorespiratory responses to submaximal exercise at high altitude, a 2024 study in Wilderness & Environmental Medicine ('Women at Altitude') examined menstrual-cycle phase, menopause, and exogenous progesterone in relation to acute mountain sickness, and a newer review ('Hormonal status and reproductive life-course states as modulators of women's physiological responses to acute and chronic hypoxia') explicitly covers menstrual cycle, contraception, pregnancy, and menopause effects on hypoxic responses. These sources address menstrual cycle and menopause effects on acute responses and AMS risk fairly directly, but the deeper cardiometabolic and long-term acclimatization data - especially for pregnancy and for chronic/long-term high-altitude residents - remains comparatively sparse and is described in these same recent papers as still needing more research.

paper.title: Knee health and associations with female-specific health, physical, psychological and social-gendered factors in women runners: the TRAIL-W cohort study protocol.

problem.title: Women runners face higher risk of knee injury and worse outcomes after knee surgery than men, but the reasons are poorly understood.
problem.summary: Women runners are more likely than men to sustain running-related injuries such as bone stress and knee injuries, and after serious knee injury and surgery they experience worse knee and health-related outcomes. Little is known about how female-specific health, physical, psychological and social-gendered factors intersect with knee health in women runners, with or without a history of knee surgery.
problem.affected_women: Women runners, including those with and without a history of knee surgery.

data_need.description: Data on how female-specific health, physical, psychological and social-gendered factors relate to knee symptoms, structural knee features, running load and running-related pain in women runners.
data_need.why_it_matters: Without this data, clinicians and researchers cannot explain why women runners have higher injury rates and worse post-surgical outcomes, limiting the ability to design effective prevention or treatment approaches tailored to women.

gap_evidence.note: The abstract states that 'little is known about the intersection of female-specific health, physical, psychological and social-gendered factors with knee health in women runners with and without a history of knee surgery,' and that the study aims to 'address critical research gaps by describing and exploring the diverse factors that may influence women runners' knee health.'

dataset_source.note: TRAIL-W is a protocol for a nested cohort study within the TRAIL (TRAjectory of knee heaLth in runners) prospective cohort in Australia, designed to comprehensively collect the needed female-specific and gendered factors alongside knee health, running load and pain data in women runners. It covers only TRAIL cohort participants (Australia-based recruitment) and, as of the search, only the study protocol has been published — actual results/data analyses addressing the research questions had not yet appeared in the literature.

collection_guidance.note: Data to be collected from active TRAIL cohort female (and male, for comparison) participants via a once-off TRAIL-W survey covering psychological, social gendered and, for women, female-specific health factors, plus a laboratory assessment measuring body composition, bone mineral density and blood biomarkers, and qualitative interviews with a subset of women runners.

verification.findings: The exact gap has been addressed by the launch of the TRAIL-W cohort study protocol (published in BMJ Open Sport & Exercise Medicine), a nested study within the existing TRAIL prospective cohort of runners, explicitly designed to collect data on 'female-specific health, physical, psychological and social gendered' factors alongside knee symptoms, structural knee features, device-measured running load and running-related pain in women runners. This is the same research group's follow-up to the gap they identified, meaning data collection is now underway or planned via TRAIL-W's nested surveys and imaging alongside TRAIL's 6-monthly assessments, but this is a study protocol paper, not yet a results/findings paper, so the actual dataset and analysed findings are not yet published.

paper.title: The effects of androgens on drug metabolism and transport: clinical pharmacologic considerations for people assigned female at birth.
paper.journal: Expert opinion on drug metabolism & toxicology

problem.title: It is unclear how testosterone and androgen-rich conditions affect drug metabolism and transport in people assigned female at birth
problem.summary: Endogenous and exogenous androgens affect health outcomes across life in people assigned female at birth, but little is known about how exogenous testosterone or androgen-rich conditions like PCOS affect how drugs are metabolized and transported. A narrative synthesis of in vivo evidence found this area remains understudied.
problem.affected_women: Cisgender women and transgender people assigned female at birth, including those with polycystic ovary syndrome or using exogenous testosterone

data_need.description: Clinical pharmacology data on how testosterone and androgen-rich conditions affect drug-metabolizing enzymes and transporters in people assigned female at birth
data_need.why_it_matters: Without this data, clinicians lack evidence to guide drug dosing and safety for cisgender women and transgender people exposed to exogenous testosterone or androgen-rich conditions.

gap_evidence.note: The abstract states that 'the effects of testosterone and other androgens on drug metabolism and transport remain understudied in people assigned female at birth' and calls for well-designed probe-substrate studies and use of prescribed medications as clinical probes of relevant enzymes and transporters.

collection_guidance.note: Investigators should use well-designed probe-substrate studies when feasible, and use prescribed medications as clinical probes of relevant drug-metabolizing enzymes and transporters, in cisgender women and transgender people.

verification.findings: Web search tools were unavailable for this query in this session (repeated tool-limit errors prevented any live search from completing), so no confirmed new dataset can be verified. Based on prior knowledge of the field, dedicated clinical pharmacology studies systematically probing how testosterone or androgen-rich states (e.g., PCOS, gender-affirming hormone therapy) alter CYP450 enzyme activity or drug transporter function specifically in people assigned female at birth remain sparse and fragmented; most existing work on gender-affirming hormone therapy pharmacology focuses on hormone levels themselves rather than their downstream effects on other drugs' metabolism. No comprehensive, well-designed probe-substrate dataset addressing this exact gap could be identified or confirmed.

paper.title: "Left Out at the Kitchen Table": Exploring Peer Support Needs Among Women Firefighters.

problem.title: Peer support programs in the fire service are not tailored to the mental health needs of women firefighters.
problem.summary: Women firefighters can have behavioral health outcomes similar to men in supportive environments, but rates of depression, anxiety, and PTSD rise sharply amid workplace discrimination and exclusion. These issues are often treated as HR matters rather than health and safety concerns. Little is known about how peer support resources, increasingly used in fire services, could be adapted to women's needs.
problem.affected_women: Women firefighters and fire service stakeholders in the United States

data_need.description: Systematic data on women firefighters' perceptions, barriers, and preferences regarding peer support programs
data_need.why_it_matters: Without this data, peer support programs may fail to build trust and psychological safety for women firefighters, leaving mental health needs unmet and risks like depression, anxiety, and PTSD unaddressed.

gap_evidence.note: The abstract states that 'despite the growing adoption of peer support programs in the fire service, little is known about how these resources can be tailored to the needs of women firefighters,' motivating the qualitative interview study described.

dataset_source.note: Qualitative interview study (35 participants: women firefighters across ranks plus fire service stakeholders) recruited via the Fire Fighter Cancer Cohort Study, covering perceptions of peer support, barriers to engagement, trust/comfort, and preferred communication strategies in the US fire service. It is qualitative rather than a large quantitative survey, so it may not capture prevalence rates or be generalizable to all departments, but it directly targets the identified gap.

collection_guidance.note: Researchers conducted semi-structured interviews with 35 women firefighters and key fire service stakeholders across the United States, exploring perceptions of peer support, barriers to engagement, trust and comfort, and preferred communication and messaging strategies.

verification.findings: A qualitative study, published in 2026 in the American Journal of Industrial Medicine (Hollerbach et al., "Left Out at the Kitchen Table": Exploring Peer Support Needs Among Women Firefighters), directly addresses this gap. Researchers conducted 35 semi-structured interviews with women firefighters and fire service stakeholders across the United States, exploring "perceptions of peer support, barriers to engagement, trust and comfort within peer support networks, and preferred communication and messaging strategies." Thematic analysis identified seven key domains including barriers to support, effective messaging, gendered workplace dynamics, resource needs, leadership influence, and stress relief strategies, providing the systematic data on perceptions, barriers, and preferences that the original paper called missing.

paper.title: Health and Health Care Access Among Afghan Refugee Women in the United States.

problem.title: Afghan refugee women in the US face multilayered barriers to health and health care access after resettlement
problem.summary: Afghan refugee women face compounded health risks from sociocultural restrictions, low literacy, forced displacement, and limited health care access, yet little is known about their experiences with health care after resettlement in the US. A qualitative study found barriers including inadequate interpretation, patriarchal norms limiting autonomy, structural barriers leading to home remedy use, sociocultural barriers to sexual and reproductive health, and unmet mental health needs.
problem.affected_women: Afghan refugee women resettled in the US, in this study aged 19-55 and residing in the San Francisco Bay Area

data_need.description: Systematic data on Afghan refugee women's health care experiences and access barriers after US resettlement is missing
data_need.why_it_matters: Without understanding these barriers, culturally sensitive and linguistically appropriate interventions cannot be designed, leaving structural deficiencies in access unaddressed.

gap_evidence.note: The abstract states that 'yet little is known about their experiences with health care after resettlement in the US,' motivating this qualitative exploration of health and health care access issues among Afghan refugee women.
gap_evidence.region: United States (San Francisco Bay Area, California)

dataset_source.note: CDC's Afghan refugee health guidance/profile and RAND Corporation surveys of Afghan evacuees cover general refugee health and resettlement experiences, including some health system contact points, but do not provide the qualitative, gender-specific data on Afghan women's health care experiences, cultural/linguistic access barriers, or maternal health needs that the original study sought to fill. They are broader population surveys, not focused qualitative research on women's care-seeking barriers.

collection_guidance.note: Semistructured interviews in Dari or English with self-identified Afghan women born outside the US, aged 18 or older, recruited via convenience and purposive sampling through refugee-serving community organizations and word of mouth until data saturation was reached; Dari interviews interpreted and validated by bilingual investigators and reviewed with an Afghan immigrant community member for accuracy.

verification.findings: A fresh web search could not be completed in this session due to a tool-use limit, so this answer relies on knowledge of publicly known post-2021 resettlement research rather than a live confirmed search. Following the 2021 Operation Allies Welcome evacuation, RAND Corporation and other resettlement-focused organizations produced broader surveys (e.g., RAND's 'Life After Resettlement' work on Afghan evacuees) and CDC published an Afghan refugee health profile/screening guidance, but these are largely quantitative or clinical-screening focused rather than qualitative studies specifically on Afghan refugee women's health care experiences and access barriers. No dataset specifically replicating or systematically extending the qualitative Bay Area study on Afghan refugee women's health care access barriers was confirmed.

paper.title: Male breast cancer: from extrapolated practice to evidence-based care.

problem.title: Men with breast cancer are treated using evidence extrapolated from studies of women, with no dedicated evidence base for their care.
problem.summary: Male breast cancer makes up about 1% of all breast cancer cases and remains understudied. Its management continues to rely on evidence extrapolated from female-focused studies. Men are typically diagnosed later, with more advanced disease, and experience worse outcomes than women, with underutilization of guideline-recommended therapies.
problem.affected_women: Not applicable; this source concerns male breast cancer patients.

data_need.description: Prospective, male-specific clinical trial data on breast cancer diagnosis, treatment sequencing, and outcomes.
data_need.why_it_matters: Without male-specific data, treatment decisions rely on extrapolation from female patients, leaving uncertainty about systemic therapy choice and sequencing and contributing to worse outcomes for men.

gap_evidence.note: The abstract states there is a 'paucity of male-specific prospective data' and highlights 'the need to significantly improve male representation in future BC trials,' noting that management 'continues to rely on evidence extrapolated from studies focused on female patients.'

dataset_source.note: The International Male Breast Cancer Program (EORTC 10085/TBCRC/BIG/NABCG) prospective cohort collects real-world data on newly diagnosed male breast cancer patients' characteristics, treatment, and outcomes internationally. It does not cover randomized comparisons of treatment sequencing/systemic therapy choice, and enrollment numbers remain small relative to female breast cancer trial populations, so it only partially addresses the identified gap.

verification.findings: Search access was unavailable for verification this session, but based on established knowledge, the International Male Breast Cancer Program (a collaboration of EORTC, BIG, TBCRC, and NABCG) includes a prospective observational component that has enrolled newly diagnosed male breast cancer patients since around 2014, collecting data on tumor characteristics, treatment patterns, and outcomes. This program has published findings (e.g., in JCO and related journals) on systemic therapy use and adjuvant endocrine therapy adherence in men, partially filling the evidence gap described. However, this is an international observational registry rather than a randomized or interventional clinical trial, has a much smaller sample size than female breast cancer trials, and does not provide the kind of prospective trial data on treatment sequencing (e.g., head-to-head comparisons of systemic therapy regimens) that would be needed to resolve uncertainty in treatment decision-making for men.
